usage: Polite; the standard line when a beauty-shop clerk offers help
반말, only with a friend, not to staff
I'd like to look on my own
Gently signals you don't need to be followed
examples: A: 뭐 찾으세요? / B: 아, 그냥 구경 좀 할게요.
A: Can I help you find something? / B: Oh, I'm just looking, thanks.
The most natural two-line exchange the moment a clerk approaches
네, 그냥 구경 좀 할게요. 필요하면 부를게요.
Yeah, just looking — I'll call you if I need help.
부를게요 ('I'll call you') politely releases them and leaves the door open
아직 안 정했어요. 혼자 좀 둘러볼게요.
I haven't decided yet — I'll just browse on my own.
Use when a clerk keeps hovering; 혼자 ('alone') is a gentle extra signal
nuance: 구경 좀 할게요 is 구경 ('looking around / sightseeing') + 좀 (softener) + 할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 'I'm going to…' volitional ending), so literally 'I'll do a little looking.' It is the polite, friendly way to tell an Olive Young or department-store beauty clerk you don't want help yet — said with a small smile, it releases social pressure without rudeness. The near-twin 그냥 둘러볼게요 is interchangeable; 구경 leans toward window-shopping while 둘러보다 emphasises walking around. For variants: add 그냥 ('just') to soften further — 그냥 구경 좀 할게요 — or replace with 혼자 좀 볼게요 to signal you want space. The English-speaker trap is rendering 'just looking' as 안 사요 ('I'm not buying'), which sounds defensive as if accusing the clerk; 구경 좀 할게요 is warm and leaves the door open. Always keep the polite -ㄹ게요 ending with staff; dropping to 구경 좀 할게 (반말) to a stranger is abrupt.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: '(I'll) do a little sightseeing.' Real meaning: 'I'm just browsing — no help needed yet.' The 구경 ('sightseeing') root makes it light and non-committal, implying casual interest rather than rejection of the clerk.

Use the moment a clerk in any beauty shop (Olive Young, brand counter, department store) asks 뭐 찾으세요? or 도와드릴까요?. This is 존댓말 and polite enough for any staff. Never drop to 구경 좀 할게 (반말) with strangers — save that for browsing with a friend.

그냥 둘러볼게요 ('I'll just browse around') is the closest twin — both are natural; 구경 frames it as 'looking around like a visitor', 둘러보다 frames it as 'walking and scanning.' 그냥만 볼게요 is also heard but slightly more blunt. All three are polite; choose any.

Softer: 그냥 구경 좀 할게요 (adding 그냥 'just'). Stronger: 혼자 좀 볼게요 ('I'd like to look alone') signals actively wanting space. To add a follow-up: 구경 좀 하다가 필요하면 부를게요 ('I'll look around and call you if I need anything').

Translating 'just looking' as 안 사요 ('I'm not buying') sounds cold and defensive, as if accusing the clerk of pressuring you. 구경 좀 할게요 keeps the warmth and leaves the interaction open. Also avoid 저 그냥요 ('just… me') which is incomplete and odd.

mistakes: Saying 안 사요 to mean 'just looking'.
안 사요 means 'I'm not buying' and sounds blunt or defensive to a clerk. The friendly, face-saving line is 구경 좀 할게요 — it doesn't shut them down, just postpones help.
Dropping 요 and saying 구경 좀 할게 to staff.
That's 반말 and sounds abrupt to a stranger. Keep the polite ending: 구경 좀 할게요.
Using 보다 alone as 좀 볼게요 expecting it to be clear.
좀 볼게요 ('I'll take a look') can sound like you want to look at one specific item the clerk is holding. For browsing the store, say 구경 좀 할게요 or 둘러볼게요.

english: Can I try this on (apply a sample)?
usage: Polite; asking to test a sample on your skin
반말, with a friend, not staff
Can I try it on the back of my hand?
손등 ('back of the hand') = where you swatch makeup
examples: A: 이거 발라봐도 돼요? / B: 네, 여기 테스터 있어요.
A: Can I try this on? / B: Yes, we have a tester right here.
The standard two-turn exchange at a cosmetics counter
립스틱 색 보려고요. 손등에 발라봐도 돼요?
I want to see the lipstick color — can I swatch it on my hand?
손등 is the normal swatch spot; naming it sounds experienced
이 선크림 끈적이는지 발라봐도 돼요?
Can I try this sunscreen to see if it's sticky?
끈적이다 ('to be sticky/tacky') states exactly what you're checking
nuance: 이거 발라봐도 돼요? breaks down as 이거 ('this') + 발라보다 (바르다 'to apply/spread on skin' + -아 보다 'try doing') + -도 돼요? ('is it okay to…?'), meaning 'is it okay if I try applying this?' The -아 보다 form signals a trial attempt, so the phrase captures both the action and its tentative feel perfectly. 바르다 is the specific verb for spreading skincare or makeup onto skin (cream, sunscreen, lip balm, tinted moisturiser); it is distinct from 칠하다 ('to paint/coat', used for walls or nail polish) — using 칠하다 for face cream sounds odd, like painting yourself. The 손등 (back of the hand) is the culturally standard swatch location, so specifying it sounds like a regular. Variants: 테스터 있어요? ('Is there a tester?') asks the same thing more simply. In 반말 with a friend: 발라봐도 돼?. The English-speaker error is asking 이거 해 봐도 돼요? ('can I try doing this?') — 해 보다 is too generic for skin application; use 발라보다.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 'Is it okay to try applying this?' The compound 발라보다 = 바르다 ('spread on skin') + -아 보다 ('try doing'), so it captures both the action and the trial nature in one verb. The real meaning: 'May I swatch or test this product on my skin?'
Said in any beauty shop when you spot a tester or sealed product and want to try it on skin. This is 존댓말 and fits all staff interactions. With a friend in 반말: 발라봐도 돼?. Do NOT use 반말 with store staff.

테스터 있어요? asks 'is there a tester?' (existence question), while 발라봐도 돼요? asks permission to apply (action question). 이거 써봐도 돼요? ('can I try using this?') is vaguer — 쓰다 can mean use in any sense; 발라보다 is precise for skin application.

Add a body part: 손등에 발라봐도 돼요? (hand back), 팔에 발라봐도 돼요? (arm). To explain why: 색 보려고요, 발라봐도 돼요? ('I want to check the color'). Stronger: 잠깐 발라봐도 될까요? ('may I just apply it briefly?') — -ㄹ까요? is slightly more tentative than -도 돼요?.

The error is using 이거 해 봐도 돼요? — 해 보다 ('try doing') is too vague for putting product on skin. The precise verb is 발라보다. Also watch the particle for the body part: apply TO a surface uses 에 (손등에 발라요), not 을/를 — 손등을 발라봐도 돼요? makes it sound like you're applying the hand itself.

mistakes: Using 칠하다 for applying cream or sunscreen.
칠하다 means 'to paint/coat' (walls, a fence). Skincare and makeup go on with 바르다. Say 발라봐도 돼요?, not 칠해 봐도 돼요?.
Saying 이거 해 봐도 돼요? to test a sample.
해 보다 ('try doing') is too vague for putting product on skin. The specific verb is 발라보다: 이거 발라봐도 돼요?
Marking the body part with 을/를: 손등을 발라봐도 돼요?
You apply product TO a surface, so the particle is 에: 손등에 발라봐도 돼요? (손등을 would mean you're applying the hand itself).

usage: Polite; the everyday ask at any beauty counter
Could I get a few more samples?
Add 더 ('more') when they give you one or two
Could you throw in some samples?
챙기다 ('to gather/pack for someone') sounds natural and warm
Slightly more tentative; asks if it's possible at all
examples: 이거 살게요. 샘플 좀 챙겨 주세요.
I'll take this — could you throw in some samples?
Buying then asking is the natural order; 챙겨 주세요 sounds warmly personal
A: 샘플 좀 주세요. / B: 네, 어떤 제품 써 보고 싶으세요?
A: Could I get some samples? / B: Sure, which products would you like to try?
Staff often ask which type you'd like — be ready to name them
혹시 이 크림 샘플 있으면 좀 주세요. 먼저 써보고 싶어서요.
If you have a sample of this cream, could I get one? I want to try it first.
혹시 ('by any chance') + a polite reason makes the ask feel natural
nuance: 샘플 좀 주세요 is 샘플 (loanword 'sample') + 좀 (softener) + 주세요 ('please give'). Sample culture in Korea is enormous — beauty staff routinely tuck free sachets into your bag especially after a purchase, so this is a routine, expected request. The warmest-sounding version uses 챙기다 ('to thoughtfully gather and pack for someone'): 샘플 좀 챙겨 주세요 feels more personal and less transactional than plain 주세요. You must know the three related words: 샘플 (free take-home sachet), 테스터 (open in-store display you swatch but don't take), and 증정품/사은품 (gift-with-purchase freebie, often full-size). Asking for the wrong one gets you the wrong answer. Variants: 더 주세요 adds 'more'; 받을 수 있어요? is slightly more tentative. The English-speaker error is adding 무료 as in 무료 샘플 주세요 — 샘플 already implies free, and adding 무료 can sound slightly grabby. Another pitfall: don't ask before buying as if entitled — Koreans usually buy first, then ask, and 좀 keeps the tone gracious.

structuredNuance.t: 'Please give me some samples.' The 좀 is crucial — it softens from a demand to a gentle request. The real social meaning is a collaborative, warm ask that fits Korean beauty culture where sampling is expected and welcomed.

Typically said at checkout after buying something — that's the cultural norm. You CAN ask before buying but add 먼저 써보고 싶어서요 ('I want to try it first') to explain. 존댓말 always with staff. With a close friend browsing together: 샘플 좀 달라고 해봐 ('ask them for samples').

샘플 (free sachet to take home) vs. 테스터 (open display to swatch in-store, cannot take) vs. 증정품/사은품 (gift-with-purchase, often full-size). Asking for a 테스터 when you want samples to take home, or vice versa, will confuse staff.
Basic: 샘플 좀 주세요. Warmer: 샘플 좀 챙겨 주세요. Tentative: 샘플 받을 수 있어요? Add 'more': 샘플 좀 더 주세요. Specific product: 이 크림 샘플 좀 주세요.
Adding 무료 ('free') sounds redundant and slightly pushy since 샘플 already implies free. Just say 샘플 좀 주세요. Also don't say 샘플 줘 to staff — 줘 is 반말 and abrupt; use 주세요 or the warmer 챙겨 주세요.

mistakes: Confusing 샘플 with 테스터.
샘플 is the free take-home sachet; 테스터 is the open in-store display you swatch but can't take. To take some home, ask for 샘플, not 테스터.
Adding 무료 as in 무료 샘플 주세요.
샘플 already implies it's free; tacking on 무료 ('free') sounds a bit grabby. Just say 샘플 좀 주세요.
Saying 샘플 줘 to staff.
줘 is 반말 and too casual for a clerk. Use 주세요 (or warmer 챙겨 주세요): 샘플 좀 주세요.

usage: Polite; telling staff your skin type
지성 = oily; swap in for your type
민감성 ('sensitive') + 라서요 to explain a need
examples: A: 피부 타입이 어떻게 되세요? / B: 저 건성이에요. 보습 잘 되는 거 찾아요.
A: What's your skin type? / B: Dry. I'm looking for something moisturizing.
The exact clerk question and ideal answer in two lines
저 건성이라 보습되는 거 찾아요.
I have dry skin, so I'm looking for something moisturizing.
건성이라 ('since I'm dry') + the product need in one natural sentence
여름엔 지성인데 겨울엔 건성이에요. 복합성인가 봐요.
I'm oily in summer but dry in winter — I guess I'm combination.
Describing how your skin shifts by season; an extremely common Korean experience
nuance: 저 피부가 건성이에요 is 저 ('I', humble) + 피부 ('skin') + 가 (subject particle) + 건성 ('dry-type', Sino-Korean 乾性) + 이에요 (polite copula). Korean names skin types with the -성 ('-type/-natured') suffix: 건성 (dry), 지성 (oily), 복합성 (combination), 민감성 (sensitive), 중성 (normal). These are the exact labels beauty staff use when they ask 피부 타입이 어떻게 되세요?. A critical distinction: 건성 is the skin-type NOUN ('dry-type'), while 건조하다 is the ADJECTIVE 'to feel dry right now' — so your constitutional type is 건성이에요, but if your skin feels parched today you'd say 피부가 건조해요. Saying 저 건조성이에요 is wrong; the type word is 건성. The most natural shortcut in-shop is 저 건성이에요 (dropping 피부가), which sounds natural and brisk. The English-speaker error is translating 'dry skin' literally as 마른 피부 — 마르다 means 'thin/skinny (body)' or 'dried out (laundry)', never a skin type. Always keep 피부가 with the subject particle 가.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'My skin is dry-type.' 건성 (乾性) is not an adjective but a noun — 'dry-nature/type'. You're classifying your skin into a Sino-Korean typology, not just describing a sensation. The real-world use is telling staff your type so they can filter recommendations.
Said whenever a clerk or dermatologist asks your skin type. The full form 저 피부가 건성이에요 is polite 존댓말. In quick shop conversation, 저 건성이에요 (dropping 피부가) is equally natural. Never use 반말 with staff.

건성이에요 (type noun, permanent classification) vs. 피부가 건조해요 (adjective, 'feels dry right now'). Don't say 건조성이에요 — that's a non-word mixing type suffix -성 onto the adjective stem 건조. The -성 type set is: 건성·지성·복합성·민감성·중성.
Shortened: 저 건성이에요. With reason: 저 건성이라 보습 제품 찾아요 ('because I'm dry, I'm looking for moisturizing products'). Conditional: 민감성이라서요 adds a reason why you need something gentle.

Translating 'dry skin' as 마른 피부 is the top error — 마르다 means 'thin/lean (body)' or 'dry (laundry)', never a skin-type. Also: using 을/를 on 피부 is ungrammatical here; it's the subject so it takes 가: 피부가 건성이에요.

mistakes: Saying 마른 피부 for 'dry skin'.
마르다 means 'thin (body)' or 'dried (laundry)'. The skin-type word is 건성. Say 저 건성이에요 or 피부가 건성이에요, never 마른 피부.
Confusing the type noun 건성 with the adjective 건조하다.
건성 = your skin TYPE ('dry-type'); 건조하다 = a condition ('feels dry now'). Type: 건성이에요. Condition: 피부가 건조해요. Don't say 건조성.
Using 을/를 on 피부.
피부 is the subject here, so use 가: 피부가 건성이에요. 피부를 건성이에요 is ungrammatical.

usage: What skin type is this for?
Polite; asking which skin a product suits
-용 ('for use by') checks a specific type fast
Can oily skin use this too?
도 ('also') asks if your type is included
examples: A: 이거 무슨 타입이에요? / B: 건성·복합성 피부에 맞는 거예요.
A: What skin type is this for? / B: It's for dry and combination skin.
The open question and a typical staff answer
저 지성인데 이거 지성용이에요?
I'm oily — is this for oily skin?
State your type then check with -용 for a quick yes/no
이 토너 민감성 피부에 써도 괜찮아요?
Is this toner okay for sensitive skin?
괜찮아요 ('is it okay') softens a safety-compatibility question
nuance: 이거 무슨 타입이에요? is 이거 ('this') + 무슨 ('what kind of') + 타입 (loanword 'type') + 이에요?, asking which skin type a product targets. In practice the most efficient real-shop phrasing uses the suffix -용 ('for the use of'): 건성용 ('for dry skin'), 지성용 ('for oily'), 민감성용 ('for sensitive') — so 이거 건성용이에요? gets a yes/no instantly. The dividing line: 무슨 타입이에요? is open-ended, while -용이에요? pins down your specific type. For the interrogative pair 무슨 vs. 어떤: 무슨 asks 'what category?' (identity), 어떤 asks 'what is it like?' (quality), and while both work here, 무슨 타입 is the fixed collocation. An even more contextual phrasing is 이거 어떤 피부에 맞아요? — 맞다 ('to fit/suit') frames it as compatibility. The English-speaker error is asking 이거 뭐에 써요? ('what do you use this for?'), which asks the product's purpose (face vs. body, morning vs. night), not skin type. To ask about skin type, say 무슨 타입이에요? or 무슨 피부용이에요?.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'This — what type is it?' The real meaning is 'which skin type does this product target?' 타입 here is specifically skin type from the standard 건성/지성/복합성/민감성/중성 set — not any general 'type.'

Said while holding a product at a beauty shelf or counter. 존댓말 with staff at all times. This phrasing is neutral and suits any formality level; with friends browsing together you could say 이거 무슨 타입이야? (반말).
무슨 타입이에요? is open-ended. -용이에요? (e.g., 건성용이에요?) is a closed yes/no. 어떤 피부에 맞아요? ('what skin does it suit?') focuses on compatibility. For speed, -용 wins; for open discovery, 무슨 타입이에요? is natural.
Shortened: 지성용이에요? Expanded: 모든 피부 타입에 써도 돼요? ('is it okay for all skin types?'). With context: 저 민감성인데 이거 써도 돼요? ('I'm sensitive — can I use this?')
이거 뭐에 써요? asks the product's PURPOSE ('what do you use it for?') — face? body? makeup removal? — not skin type. For skin type always say 무슨 타입이에요? or 무슨 피부용이에요?.

mistakes: Asking 이거 뭐에 써요? to mean 'what skin type'.
That asks the product's purpose (face? body?), not skin type. For skin type, ask 이거 무슨 타입이에요? or 무슨 피부용이에요?
Saying 건성을 위한 거예요? instead of 건성용.
건성을 위한 거 is grammatical but clunky. Koreans use the compact suffix -용: 이거 건성용이에요?
Mixing 무슨 and 어떤 wrongly with 타입.
The fixed collocation is 무슨 타입. 어떤 타입 is understandable but less idiomatic for asking the category; default to 무슨 타입이에요?

english: Do you have something really moisturizing?
usage: Polite; asking for a hydrating product
촉촉하다 ('moist, dewy') — the sensory feel you want
속건조 = 'inner dryness' under an oily surface
examples: A: 어떤 거 찾으세요? / B: 겨울이라 너무 당겨요. 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요?
A: What are you looking for? / B: My skin feels so tight in winter — do you have something really moisturizing?
당기다 ('feel tight/taut') is the classic dry-skin complaint; this is the natural two-turn exchange
저 지성인데 속건조가 심해요. 촉촉하면서 안 무거운 거 추천해 주세요.
I'm oily but really dehydrated underneath — something hydrating but not heavy, please.
The classic oily-but-dehydrated combination request
보습력 좋은 거로 추천해 주세요. 크림 말고 세럼도 괜찮아요.
Recommend something with good moisture retention — a serum is fine too, not just a cream.
보습력 + opening up the format shows you know skincare categories
nuance: 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요? is 보습 ('moisture retention', Sino-Korean 保濕) + 잘 되는 ('that works well at it') + 거 ('thing') + 있어요? ('do you have?'). 보습 is THE key beauty noun for hydration and moisturizing; the product quality is 보습력 ('moisturizing power'), and the sensory result is 촉촉하다 ('dewy, moist'). A critical real-life concept is 속건조 ('inner dryness') — skin that's oily on the surface but parched underneath, extremely common in Korea and something you can name to get precisely the right lightweight product. The dryness sensation is 당기다 ('to feel tight/taut'): 당겨요 = 'my skin feels taut.' The variant 촉촉한 거 있어요? focuses on the desired sensory outcome rather than the product function. The English-speaker trap is using 수분 and 보습 interchangeably: 수분 is 'water/moisture (the substance)', 보습 is 'retention of that moisture' — you can say 수분 크림 ('moisture cream') for a product name, but to ask generally for moisturizing, 보습 잘 되는 거 is the natural phrasing. Never use 젖은 거 ('wet/soggy thing') for 'moist/dewy' — that sounds unpleasant.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Is there something that does moisture-retention well?' 보습 (保濕) = 'protect/retain moisture.' Real meaning: 'Do you have a strongly hydrating product?' The 잘 되는 frame ('works well at it') is a natural Korean way to ask for a product with a specific effective quality.

Said to a beauty shop clerk when your skin is dry, tight, or you're entering a dry season. 존댓말 for all staff. The whole …는 거 있어요? template ('do you have something that…?') is the all-purpose shop request frame and sounds natural at any counter.

보습 잘 되는 거 (function focus: 'retains moisture well') vs. 촉촉한 거 (sensory focus: 'feels dewy/moist'). You'd use 보습 when talking to a knowledgeable clerk; 촉촉하다 is more emotional and descriptive. 보습력 좋은 거로 추천해 주세요 asks for a specific recommendation.
보습 is Sino-Korean 保濕: 보 (保) = 'protect/keep', 습 (濕) = 'moisture/dampness'. 보습력 adds 력 (力) = 'power/strength', so 'moisturizing power.'

수분 ('water/moisture the substance') and 보습 ('retention of moisture') are different: 수분 크림 is a product category name, but asking generally for moisturizing uses 보습 잘 되는 거. Also: 젖은 거 ('wet/soggy thing') for 'moist skin feel' sounds unpleasant — the right word is 촉촉하다.

mistakes: Saying 젖은 거 for 'moist/dewy'.
젖다 means 'wet, soggy' (like wet hair). Dewy skin is 촉촉하다. Ask for 촉촉한 거, not 젖은 거.
Confusing the sensation 당기다 with 당기다 'to crave'.
피부가 당기다 = 'skin feels tight (dry)'; 입맛이 당기다 = 'to have an appetite'. For dry skin, 피부가 당겨요 means it feels taut — use it to describe dryness.
Asking 물 많은 거 있어요? for hydration.
물 많은 거 ('something with lots of water') sounds odd for skincare. Use 보습 잘 되는 거 or 수분 크림 / 촉촉한 거.

usage: Polite, full formal term for sunscreen
선크림 (loanword) is what people actually say day-to-day
Not the cream — do you have a sun stick?
선스틱 ('sun stick') for the twist-up format
examples: A: 어디 있어요? / B: 선크림이요? 저쪽 자외선 차단제 코너에 있어요.
A: Where is it? / B: Sunscreen? It's over at the UV-protection corner.
Typical clerk redirect; note both 선크림 and 자외선 차단제 used in one exchange
얼굴에 바르는 선크림 찾는데 어디 있어요?
I'm looking for facial sunscreen — where is it?
얼굴에 바르는 ('the kind for the face') narrows the search away from body sunscreen
에스피에프 높은 선크림 있어요? 바닷가 가서요.
Do you have high-SPF sunscreen? I'm going to the beach.
SPF (에스피에프) + reason makes the request concrete and helps staff pick the right product
nuance: 자외선 차단제 어디 있어요? is 자외선 ('ultraviolet rays', Sino-Korean 紫外線) + 차단제 ('blocking agent': 차단 'block' + 제 'agent') + 어디 있어요? ('where is it?'). 자외선 차단제 is the full, formal, on-the-label term, but in daily speech everyone says 선크림 — staff understand either, and 선크림 sounds relaxed and natural. Formats have distinct names you need: 선크림 (cream), 선스틱 (twist-up stick), 선쿠션 (cushion-compact), 선스프레이 (spray). The distinction 자외선 차단 ('UV blocking' — the function) vs. 자외선 차단제 ('the product') matters: drop the 제 and you've named the feature, not the item — keep 차단제 or just say 선크림. Regarding SPF: Koreans read the abbreviation as 에스피에프 (Korean letter-names) plus the Sino-Korean number: SPF 50 = 에스피에프 오십. Saying the English 'es-pee-ef fifty' may not be understood. Default 존댓말; 어디 있어요? is the polite location question.

structuredNuance.t: 자외선 차단제 = 'ultraviolet-ray blocking agent' (literal). Real meaning and daily use: 선크림. Staff expect either, but 선크림 is what virtually everyone actually says when shopping.
Said in any cosmetics shop, pharmacy (약국), or convenience store sunscreen section. 존댓말 with staff. With friends: 선크림 어딨어? (반말). The formal 자외선 차단제 is more for labels, packaging, or formal writing.
자외선 차단제 (formal, on-label) = 선크림 (daily loanword, most common) = 선블록 (less common loanword variant). 차단제 (the product) vs. 차단 (the function/feature) — keep the 제 when asking for the product itself.
자외선 is Sino-Korean 紫外線 ('purple-outside rays' = ultraviolet); 차단 (遮斷) = 'to block/cut off'; 제 (劑) = 'agent/preparation'. Together: 'UV-ray-blocking agent.'
SPF is read as 에스피에프 not English initials — saying 'es-pee-ef' may not land. SPF 50 = 에스피에프 오십. Also: 햇빛 크림 ('sunlight cream') is not a word in Korean skincare — always say 선크림 or 자외선 차단제.

mistakes: Saying 햇빛 크림 ('sunlight cream') for sunscreen.
There's no such word. It's 선크림 or formally 자외선 차단제. 햇빛 크림 won't be understood as a product.
Dropping 제 and saying 자외선 차단 있어요?
자외선 차단 names the function ('UV blocking'), not the product. To buy the item, say 자외선 차단제 or, more naturally, 선크림 있어요?
Pronouncing SPF as English letters.
Koreans read it 에스피에프 plus the Sino number: SPF 50 = 에스피에프 오십. Saying 'es-pee-eff fifty' in English may not land; use 에스피에프 오십.

usage: Isn't this heavy on the skin?
Polite; checking if a cream feels heavy
끈적이다 ('to be tacky/sticky') — a key texture worry
How does it feel going on?
발리다 (passive of 바르다) asks about the application texture
Is it on the lighter/fresher side?
산뜻하다 ('fresh, light') = the opposite of heavy
examples: A: 이거 발라봐도 돼요? / B: 네. 이거 안 무거워요? / A: 생각보다 산뜻해요.
A: Can I try this? / B: Sure. Isn't it heavy? / A: It's lighter than I expected.
A real three-turn testing conversation around texture
여름엔 무거운 게 싫어요. 이거 안 끈적여요?
I don't like heavy stuff in summer — isn't this sticky?
끈적이다 is the top summer texture complaint for sunscreen and cream
촉촉한데 산뜻하면 좋겠어요. 이거 발리는 느낌 어때요?
I want hydrating but light — how does this feel going on?
발림성 ('application feel') is what you're really asking about here
nuance: 이거 안 무거워요? is 이거 ('this') + 안 ('not') + 무겁다 ('to be heavy') in polite question form — the 안 …요? structure voices a worry and invites reassurance. In skincare 무겁다 is a texture adjective meaning thick and occlusive, sitting heavily on the skin — not physical weight. Its opposites are 가볍다 ('light') and 산뜻하다 ('fresh, light, airy'). The other key texture worry is 끈적이다 ('to be sticky/tacky'), especially for sunscreen and summer products. Koreans also discuss 발림성 ('spreadability / how a product applies', from the passive 발리다 of 바르다) and 흡수 ('absorption': 잘 흡수돼요 = 'absorbs well'). The variant 산뜻한 편이에요? ('is it on the light/fresh side?') inverts the worry into a positive ask — useful for getting an encouraging answer. The English-speaker errors: (1) translating 'heavy' as 무게 있어요? — that asks about physical weight, not texture; (2) conflating 무겁다 (texture) with 기름지다/번들거리다 ('greasy/shiny' — an oily look), which is a different complaint. Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Isn't this heavy?' In skincare context 무겁다 has nothing to do with physical weight — it describes a thick, occlusive texture that sits densely on the skin. The real question is: 'Is this product too dense or clingy for everyday use?'

Said while testing or inspecting a cream, lotion, or sunscreen — especially richer formulas or winter products. The 안 …요? frame is a natural polite way to voice worry and prompt reassurance. 존댓말 with staff; 안 무거워? in 반말 with a friend.
안 무거워요? (texture is heavy/dense) vs. 안 끈적여요? (texture is sticky/tacky) vs. 번들거리지 않아요? (finish is shiny/greasy). These are three different texture concerns; be precise about which one you mean.
Inverted positive: 산뜻한 편이에요? ('is it on the lighter side?'). More explicit: 바르고 나서 답답한 느낌 없어요? ('no stuffy/suffocating feel after applying?'). Absorption ask: 잘 흡수돼요? ('does it absorb well?').

무게 있어요? asks about literal physical weight — wrong for texture. Use the adjective 무겁다 in question form: 안 무거워요?. Also don't use 무겁다 to mean 'greasy' (oily shine) — that's 번들거리다 / 기름지다; 무겁다 is about density and coverage, not shine.

mistakes: Asking 무게 있어요? for a 'heavy' feel.
무게 means physical weight. The skincare feel is the adjective 무겁다: 이거 안 무거워요? (Does it feel heavy/thick on the skin?)
Using 무겁다 to mean 'greasy'.
무겁다 is a thick, dense feel; greasy shine is 번들거리다 or 기름지다. If you mean shiny/oily, ask 번들거리지 않아요?
Confusing 끈적하다 and 끈적이다 in negative questions.

Both 끈적하다 ('to be sticky', adjective) and 끈적이다 ('to feel sticky', active verb) are used. For the natural question 'isn't it sticky?' use the verb form: 안 끈적여요? (from 끈적이다) or 안 끈적거려요? (from 끈적거리다). 끈적하지 않아요? is also correct but more bookish; 끈적여요? is the everyday shop register.

usage: Polite; asking for an in-store display tester
Is there one I can try on?
Descriptive fallback if 테스터 isn't understood
When you can't find the open display
For makeup; asks to view/swatch the shade
examples: A: 테스터 있어요? / B: 네, 여기 있어요. 손등에 발라보세요.
A: Is there a tester? / B: Yes, here it is — try it on the back of your hand.
The most natural two-turn tester exchange at any counter
이 쿠션 테스터 있어요? 색 좀 보고 싶어서요.
Is there a tester for this cushion? I want to check the shade.
색 보다 ('check the color') is the specific makeup reason
테스터 없으면 손등에라도 발라볼 수 있을까요?
If there's no tester, could I at least try it on my hand?
에라도 ('even just on…') is a polite fallback when there's no display
nuance: 테스터 있어요? is the loanword 테스터 ('tester') + 있어요? ('is there?'), asking for the open in-store display unit you can swatch without buying. This sits in a three-way vocabulary set every beauty shopper must know: 테스터 (in-store try unit, cannot take home), 샘플 (free take-home sachet), and 증정품/사은품 (gift-with-purchase freebie). Confusing these leads to misunderstandings — asking 샘플 있어요? at a lipstick display may get you a sachet to take home, not permission to swatch the shade. Korean beauty stores, especially Olive Young and brand counters, routinely have testers out, making this a routine ask. If the word 테스터 draws a blank, the descriptive fallback 발라볼 수 있는 거 있어요? ('is there something I can try on?') always works. For makeup color specifically, 색 좀 볼 수 있을까요? ('could I check the color?') is natural. The over-formal 시험용 제품 있습니까? sounds stiff and bookish — stick to 테스터 있어요?. Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Is there a tester?' The loanword 테스터 (English 'tester') is used directly. Real meaning: 'Is there an open display unit I can swatch/try on my skin right now, without buying?'

Said at any beauty counter when you want to try a product before buying — most commonly for lipstick, foundation, or skincare texture. 존댓말 with staff always. The simple 있어요? question is perfectly polite; you don't need a more complex framing.

테스터 (try in-store, cannot take) ≠ 샘플 (take-home free sachet) ≠ 증정품/사은품 (gift with purchase). These are three distinct things. Confuse 테스터 with 샘플 and you'll either get the wrong answer or leave empty-handed.
Fallback description: 발라볼 수 있는 거 있어요? Location: 테스터 어디 있어요? Color check: 색 좀 볼 수 있을까요? Polite fallback when no tester: 손등에라도 발라봐도 돼요?

Saying 샘플 있어요? when you want to swatch in-store will get you the take-home freebie, not a tester to try now. Also avoid the over-formal 시험용 제품 있습니까? — it sounds like a written form, not a shop interaction.

mistakes: Asking 샘플 있어요? when you want to swatch in-store.
샘플 is the take-home freebie. The in-store try unit is 테스터. To test a shade now, ask 테스터 있어요? or 발라볼 수 있는 거 있어요?
Confusing 테스터 with 증정품/사은품.
테스터 = in-store try unit; 증정품/사은품 = a gift with purchase. They're different things; ask for 테스터 to test, not 증정품.
Over-formal 시험용 제품 있습니까?
That's stiff and bookish. The everyday word is the loanword 테스터: 테스터 있어요?

usage: Polite; asking if a product causes breakouts
I break out easily — is this okay?
자극 ('irritation') is the key worry for reactive skin
examples: A: 이거 트러블 안 나요? / B: 네, 저자극 성분이라 괜찮아요.
A: Won't this break me out? / B: It's low-irritant ingredients, so you should be fine.
The worry-and-reassurance exchange you'll often get at a counter
저 피부 예민한데 이거 트러블 안 나요?
My skin's sensitive — won't this break me out?
예민하다 ('sensitive/touchy') describes reactive skin that flares easily
새 제품 쓰면 잘 뒤집어져서요. 자극 없는 거 맞아요?
New products often make me break out — this is non-irritating, right?
뒤집어지다 as context, then confirming 자극 없는 거 맞아요?
nuance: 이거 트러블 안 나요? is 이거 ('this') + 트러블 (Konglish 'trouble' = a skin breakout or flare-up) + 안 나요? ('doesn't it come out/appear?'). The verb 나다 ('to come out/appear') is the correct partner for both 트러블 and 여드름: 트러블이 나다 ('to have a breakout'), 여드름이 나다 ('to get a pimple'). 트러블 in beauty context strictly means a skin flare or breakout — it has nothing to do with 'trouble' in general; for a general problem use 문제. It is broader than 여드름 (specifically acne/pimples): 트러블 covers redness, small bumps, any flare. The other key worry word is 자극 ('irritation/stimulation'): 자극 없어요? = 'is it non-irritating?', 자극적이에요? = 'is it harsh?' Also vivid: 뒤집어지다 ('to flip over') is slang for skin going haywire, fine for a beauty shop but soften to 트러블이 났어요 at a clinic. The English-speaker error is translating 'break out' as 부서지다 or 깨지다 ('to shatter/break apart') — wrong verb; use 나다 with 트러블/여드름. Another trap: 자극하다 ('to stimulate/provoke someone') is wrong for 'irritating product'; say 자극적이에요? or 자극 있어요?. Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Doesn't trouble come out with this?' 트러블 is Konglish repurposed: in English 'trouble' is abstract; in Korean beauty 트러블 strictly = a skin breakout, bump, or flare. Real meaning: 'Will this product make my skin break out?'

Said before buying any new product, especially cream, foundation, or sunscreen when you have reactive skin. 존댓말 with staff. In 반말 with a friend: 이거 트러블 안 나? At a dermatology clinic, use 트러블이 났어요 or describe symptoms clinically (붉어지고 가려워요) rather than slang.

트러블 나다 (any breakout/flare, broad) vs. 여드름 나다 (acne/pimple specifically). 자극 없어요? checks irritation before use; 트러블 안 나요? checks breakout outcome. Use 자극 for ingredients, 트러블 for the resulting skin reaction.
More casual: 뒤집어지지 않을까요? With reason: 저 예민한 편이라 트러블 자주 나서요 ('I'm a bit sensitive and break out often'). Specific: 이 성분들 자극 없어요? ('are these ingredients non-irritating?')

'Break out' translates to 나다 with the skin word — 트러블이 나다, 여드름이 나다. Never use 부서지다 or 깨지다 ('shatter/break apart') — those are for objects. Also 자극하다 means 'to stimulate/provoke a person,' not 'to irritate skin'; use 자극적이에요? or 자극 없어요? for products.

mistakes: Translating 'break out' as 부서지다 or 깨지다.
Those mean 'shatter/break apart' for objects. Skin breaks out with 나다: 트러블이 나다 / 여드름이 나다. Ask 이거 트러블 안 나요?
Using 트러블 for general 'trouble/problem'.
In skincare 트러블 specifically means a skin breakout/flare. For a general problem use 문제. Here 트러블 = breakout only.
Saying 자극해요? to ask if it's irritating.
자극하다 means 'to stimulate/provoke (someone)'. For a harsh product ask 자극 있어요? / 자극적이에요?, or 자극 없어요? for non-irritating.

english: My makeup doesn't come off well
usage: My makeup doesn't come off well
Do I need to remove this with cleansing oil?
클렌징오일 for heavy or waterproof makeup
examples: A: 화장이 잘 안 지워지는데 어떻게 해야 해요? / B: 클렌징오일 먼저 쓰고 폼으로 이중 세안하면 돼요.
A: My makeup won't come off properly — what should I do? / B: Use cleansing oil first, then do double-cleansing with foam.
The key advice exchange; introduces 이중 세안 (double cleansing)
눈 화장이 잘 안 지워져요. 립앤아이 리무버 있어요?
Eye makeup won't come off — do you have a lip & eye remover?
립앤아이 리무버 is the specific product for stubborn eye and lip makeup
선크림이 안 지워지는 느낌이라 클렌징오일 쓰려고요.
My sunscreen feels like it won't wash off, so I'll use cleansing oil.
안 지워지는 느낌 ('the feeling it won't come off') is a natural compound expression
nuance: 화장 잘 안 지워져요 is 화장 ('makeup') + 잘 ('well') + 안 ('not') + 지워져요 (passive of 지우다, 'to erase/remove'). The voice distinction is crucial: 지우다 is active ('I remove makeup', 화장을 지우다), while 지워지다 is passive ('makeup comes off', 화장이 지워지다). To say it doesn't come off, you use the passive 안 지워져요; mixing voices — 화장이 안 지워요 (active verb with subject marker) — is a grammar error. The whole area of makeup removal is called 클렌징, and products divide into 클렌징오일 (oil, best for waterproof/heavy makeup), 클렌징워터 (micellar water), 클렌징폼 (foam, for general face wash), and 리무버 (point remover, especially 립앤아이 리무버). The standard Korean skincare method is 이중 세안 ('double cleansing') — oil first to dissolve makeup, then foam to cleanse the skin. The English-speaker errors: (1) 화장을 벗다 ('take off', like clothes) — 벗다 is for clothes/shoes only, never makeup; use 지우다; (2) calling everything 비누 ('soap') — makeup removal uses 클렌징 products, not 비누. Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Makeup well-not-comes-off.' The passive form 지워지다 (not the active 지우다) is key — you're saying the makeup fails to come off by itself/with effort, not that you can't actively remove it. Real meaning: 'No matter what I do, my makeup won't wash off properly.'

Said to a beauty staff member when asking for a makeup remover recommendation, or to a friend describing your skincare woes. 존댓말 with staff. The active alternative 화장을 못 지워요 ('I can't remove my makeup') puts the fault on yourself, whereas the passive 안 지워져요 puts it on the product — both are natural, but the passive is more common.
화장 잘 안 지워져요 (passive, makeup won't come off) vs. 화장을 못 지워요 (active, I can't remove it). Both are natural. 클렌징이 안 돼요 ('cleansing isn't working') is a broader form covering skin not feeling clean too.

Active: 화장을 지우다 ('to remove makeup'). Passive: 화장이 지워지다 ('makeup comes off'). Negative passive: 화장이 안 지워져요 ('makeup won't come off'). Active negative: 화장을 못 지워요 ('I can't remove the makeup'). Never mix: 화장이 안 지워요 is wrong.

'Take off makeup' as 화장을 벗다 is a direct-translation error — 벗다 is only for clothing and shoes. Makeup is always removed with 지우다. Also: calling all cleansing products 비누 ('soap') is odd; the category is 클렌징 (클렌징오일/폼/워터/리무버).

mistakes: Saying 화장을 벗다 for removing makeup.
벗다 ('take off') is for clothes/shoes. Makeup is removed with 지우다: 화장을 지우다. Never 화장을 벗다.
Mixing active/passive: 화장이 안 지워요.
With the subject 화장이, you need the passive: 화장이 안 지워져요 ('it doesn't come off'). Active would be 화장을 못 지워요 ('I can't remove it').
Calling all cleansers 비누 (soap).
Makeup removers are 클렌징 products (클렌징오일/워터/폼) or 리무버, not 비누. For removal, ask about 클렌징 or 리무버, not 비누.

usage: Polite; checking if a product is scented
무향 ('no scent') for a quick yes/no
Do you have an unscented one?
향 안 나는 거 = 'the kind with no smell'
examples: A: 이거 향 있어요? / B: 은은하게 나는 편이에요. 강하지 않아요.
A: Does this have a fragrance? / B: It's lightly scented — not strong.
The natural check-and-reassurance exchange about scent intensity
향에 좀 민감해서요. 무향인 거 있어요?
I'm a bit sensitive to fragrance — do you have a fragrance-free one?
향에 민감하다 + 무향인 거 is the most natural way to ask for scent-free skincare
향 너무 강한 건 부담스러워요. 은은한 거 있어요?
Strong scents are a bit much for me — anything subtle?
은은하다 ('faint, subtle, delicate') is exactly the scent quality you want to name
nuance: 이거 향 있어요? is 이거 ('this') + 향 ('scent/fragrance', Sino-Korean 香) + 있어요? ('is there?'). 향 is the everyday neutral word for a product's smell; the verb 'to give off a scent' is 향이 나다 (향 나요 = 'it's scented', 향 안 나요 = 'no scent'). To ask about fragrance-free products: 무향 (無香 'no scent') is the label and the word to use. Useful scent descriptors: 은은하다 ('faint, subtle'), 강하다 ('strong'), 인공적이다 ('artificial'), 자연스럽다 ('natural'). For those with sensitive skin, 향에 민감하다 ('sensitive to fragrance') gives context. Two label terms: 무향 ('no scent added') vs. 무향료 ('no fragrance ingredient'); in conversation 무향 covers both. The English-speaker error is using 냄새 — a neutral-to-negative word meaning 'odor' — for a product's fragrance: 이거 냄새 나요? sounds like 'does this stink?', mildly insulting the product. Always use 향 for pleasant or neutral product scent, and reserve 냄새 for unpleasant odors. Particle note: 향이 있어요 / 향 있어요 (both natural), never 향을 있어요. Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Is there a scent in this?' 향 (香) is a neutral-to-pleasant fragrance word. Real meaning: 'Does this product contain/give off a scent?' — often asked by people with fragrance sensitivity or those buying for sensitive skin.

Said while picking up a product at a beauty counter, pharmacy, or online consultation when you can't smell it. 존댓말 with staff. 향 있어? in 반말 with a friend is natural. Those with sensitive skin or allergies often frame the context: 향에 민감해서요 ('because I'm sensitive to fragrance').

향 (neutral/pleasant product scent) vs. 냄새 (neutral-to-negative 'odor', often unpleasant). 향기 is more poetic/literary ('a lovely fragrance'). For functional skincare questions, 향 is standard. 무향 ('fragrance-free') vs. 무향료 ('no fragrance ingredient added') are label distinctions; in conversation 무향 covers both.
향 is Sino-Korean 香 ('scent/fragrance'). 무향 is 無香 ('no scent'). 향기 (香氣) adds 기 (氣) = 'air/spirit/energy', giving a more elevated, pleasantly-airy sense.

냄새 leans negative ('odor/stink'). 이거 냄새 나요? sounds like 'does this smell bad?' Use 향 for product fragrance: 이거 향 있어요? / 향 나요?. Also don't say 향 없어 as a polite request to staff — 없어 is 반말; say 무향인 거 있어요?.

mistakes: Asking 이거 냄새 나요? to mean 'is it scented?'.
냄새 leans negative ('odor/stink'). For a product's fragrance use 향: 이거 향 있어요? / 향 나요? 냄새 나요? implies it smells bad.
Saying 향 없어 instead of 무향.
To ask for a fragrance-free product, the clean term is 무향: 무향인 거 있어요? 향 없어 (반말) is also too casual for staff.
Using 향기 vs 향 wrongly in a question.
향기 ('a (nice) fragrance/aroma') is more poetic. For the plain functional question, 향 is standard: 향 있어요?, 향 강해요?

english: What's the expiry date on this?
usage: What's the expiry date on this?
Polite; asking how long it's good for
How long does it last once opened?
개봉 후 ('after opening') = the PAO period
Gently checking it's not near expiry
It's not past its use-by, right?
사용기한 ('use-by date') for the firmer term
examples: A: 이거 유통기한 언제까지예요? / B: 내년 3월까지예요.
A: What's the expiry date on this? / B: It's good until next March.
The natural question-and-answer format for an expiry inquiry
개봉 후에 6개월 안에 써야 돼요?
Do I need to use it within 6 months of opening?
Asking about the post-opening period (PAO) — essential for serums and vitamin C products
할인하는 거 보니까 혹시 유통기한 임박이에요?
Since it's on sale — is it maybe close to expiring?
임박 ('imminent/approaching') is the exact word for near-expiry discounted stock
nuance: 이거 유통기한 언제까지예요? is 이거 ('this') + 유통기한 ('sell-by/distribution period', Sino-Korean 流通期限) + 언제까지 ('until when') + 예요?. Korean cosmetics carry two key date labels: 유통기한 (the sell-by or best-before date, what you ask about before buying) and 사용기한 ('use-by date', how long once opened — also expressed as 개봉 후 사용기간 or the PAO mark, e.g. '12M'). The word for near-expiry stock is 임박 ('imminent'), commonly seen as 유통기한 임박 상품 ('near-expiry product') on discounted items. If a product is already expired, you say 유통기한이 지났어요 ('the expiry date has passed'), using 지나다 ('to pass'). The English-speaker trap is using 만료되다 for cosmetic expiry — that's for contracts and memberships, not physical products; use 지나다. Another error: the correct temporal frame for a deadline is 언제까지예요? ('until when?'), not 언제예요? ('when is it?'), which sounds like asking a single moment in time. Keep 예요 fused: 언제까지예요, not 언제까지 예요. Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'This — the distribution time-limit — until when is it?' 유통기한 (流通期限) = the sell-by/best-before date on an unopened product. Real meaning: 'How long is this product fresh/safe to use before I even open it?'

Said at checkout or while examining a product, especially discounted items or older stock. This is 존댓말 and completely normal — Korean staff expect this question. Particularly important for vitamin C serums and active products that degrade quickly.

유통기한 (sell-by, while sealed) vs. 사용기한/개봉 후 사용기간 (use-by after opening, the PAO period). These are different questions: 유통기한 언제까지예요? before you buy; 개봉 후에 얼마나 써요? once you have it. Also 유통기한이 지났어요 ('it's expired') vs. 유통기한이 임박했어요 ('it's near expiry').
유통기한 is Sino-Korean 流通期限: 유통 (流通) = 'distribution/circulation', 기한 (期限) = 'time limit/deadline'. Literally 'distribution-time limit.'

만료되다 is for contracts/memberships expiring — not cosmetics. For product expiry say 유통기한/사용기한 + 지나다 ('to pass'). Also 언제까지예요? (deadline frame: 'until when?') is correct, not 언제예요? which asks for a single point in time.

mistakes: Using 만료되다 for product expiry.
만료되다 is for contracts/memberships expiring. For cosmetics/food say 유통기한 / 사용기한, and 지나다 for 'expired': 유통기한 지났어요?
Asking 유통기한 언제예요? instead of 언제까지예요?
A deadline takes 까지 ('until'): 언제까지예요? 언제예요? asks for a single moment and sounds off for a 'good-until' date.
Confusing 유통기한 with 개봉 후 사용기간.
유통기한 = sell-by (unopened); 개봉 후 사용기간 (PAO, e.g. 12M) = how long after opening. For 'how long once I open it', ask 개봉 후에 얼마나 써요?

english: My skin really broke out / freaked out
usage: Polite; describing a bad flare-up (슬랭 뒤집어지다)
여드름 for actual acne; 잔뜩 ('a whole lot')
examples: A: 피부 왜 이래? / B: 새 크림 썼더니 피부가 다 뒤집어졌어.
A: What's going on with your skin? / B: I used a new cream and my skin just freaked out.
A candid friend-to-friend exchange using 반말 — shows the colloquial register
새 제품 썼더니 피부가 다 뒤집어졌어요. 진정되는 거 있어요?
I used a new product and my skin freaked out — anything calming?
진정 ('calming/soothing') is the natural follow-up ask after a flare
환절기라 그런지 트러블이 심하게 나고 화끈거려요.
Maybe it's the changing season — I'm breaking out badly and it stings.
화끈거리다 ('to burn/sting') + 환절기 ('season change') is a classic Korean skin concern
nuance: 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요 is 피부 ('skin') + 가 + 너무 ('so much/too') + 뒤집어졌어요 (past of 뒤집어지다, literally 'to be turned upside down') — vivid, widely used colloquial slang for skin reacting badly, breaking out, or going haywire after a product. It is more dramatic and emotional than the neutral 트러블이 났어요 ('I broke out') and much more vivid than the clinical 여드름이 났어요. When skin is in this state, you ask for 진정 ('calming/soothing') products — 진정되는 거 ('something that calms'), 진정 에센스, 진정 크림 — since 진정 is the beauty word for soothing irritated or inflamed skin. Sensation vocabulary: 화끈거리다 ('to burn/sting'), 가렵다 ('to itch'), 붉어지다/빨개지다 ('to redden'). A very common trigger Koreans cite is 환절기 ('change of seasons'). Register note: 뒤집어지다 is informal and expressive — fine in a shop or with friends in either 존댓말 or 반말, but at a dermatology clinic lean on the neutral 트러블이 났어요 or describe symptoms directly. Particle: 피부가, never 피부를. 너무 in colloquial speech means 'really/so' (not just 'excessively').

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'My skin was completely turned upside down.' 뒤집어지다 = 'to flip over/invert' — vivid physical imagery applied to skin going haywire. Real meaning: 'My skin broke out badly / reacted horribly to a product.'

Informal but widely used — fine in a beauty shop (존댓말), with friends (반말: 피부가 완전 뒤집어졌어), or online posts. At a dermatology clinic, soften to 트러블이 심하게 났어요 or describe symptoms: 붉어지고 가려워요. Do NOT say this in formal medical or professional writing.
뒤집어지다 (vivid slang, strong reaction, any cause) > 트러블이 나다 (neutral, broad breakout) > 여드름이 나다 (clinical, acne specifically). Choose by register: clinic → 여드름/트러블, shop/friend → 뒤집어지다.
Intensified: 피부가 완전 뒤집어졌어요 ('my skin completely broke out'). Causal: 새 제품 쓰고 나서 뒤집어졌어요. Follow-up ask: 진정되는 거 있어요? / 진정 크림 추천해 주세요.
Don't take 뒤집어지다 literally as 'turned upside down' — it's pure skin-break-out slang. And never translate 'broke out' as 부서지다/깨지다 ('shatter'). The natural options are 뒤집어지다 (slang), 트러블이 나다, 여드름이 나다.

mistakes: Reading 뒤집어지다 literally as 'turn upside down'.
In skincare it's slang for skin reacting badly / breaking out. 피부가 뒤집어졌어요 = 'my skin freaked out', not anything physically flipping.
Asking for 진정시키는 거 wrongly as 진정 약.
For soothing skincare say 진정되는 거 / 진정 제품 ('calming product'). 진정 약 ('sedative') is medicine for nerves, not skin.
Using 너무 to mean simply 'very' in writing.
너무 means 'too/excessively' but colloquially also 'so'. It's fine in speech (너무 뒤집어졌어요); just know it carries an 'excessive' nuance, stronger than plain 아주.

english: Can I get a refund on this?
usage: Can I get a refund on this?
Polite; asking if a return is possible
I have the receipt — is a refund possible?
It doesn't suit my skin, so I'd like a refund
안 맞다 ('doesn't suit') = the common valid reason
examples: A: 이거 환불돼요? / B: 개봉하셨나요? 개봉 후엔 교환만 가능해요.
A: Can I get a refund on this? / B: Did you open it? After opening, exchange only.
The realistic counter-exchange — staff often redirect opened products to exchange only
한 번 발라봤는데 트러블이 나서요. 환불돼요?
I tried it once and it broke me out — can I get a refund?
Giving a specific reason (트러블) is the culturally expected approach
개봉했는데도 환불 가능해요? 피부에 안 맞아서요.
Can I still get a refund even though I opened it? It doesn't suit my skin.
개봉했는데도 ('even though I opened it') pre-empts the most common refusal reason
nuance: 이거 환불돼요? is 이거 ('this') + 환불 ('refund', Sino-Korean 還拂) + 되다 ('to be possible/doable') in polite question form — 'is a refund possible?' The 되다 construction is the civil way to ask about store policy; it asks 'is it feasible?' rather than demanding. You must know three related terms: 환불 (refund — money returned), 교환 (exchange — swapped for another item), 반품 (the act of returning goods). In practice the script often goes: ask 환불돼요? → staff ask if it's opened (개봉 여부) → if opened, they may offer 교환 only. The accepted social reason is 피부에 안 맞아서 ('because it doesn't suit my skin') or 트러블이 나서 ('because it broke me out'). Always bring the 영수증 (receipt). The English-speaker error is saying 돈 돌려주세요 ('give my money back') — blunt and confrontational. The polite ask is 환불돼요? or 환불 가능해요?, then 환불하고 싶어요 ('I'd like a refund') with a reason. Note 환불하다 is what the store does; as the customer you ask if it's possible (돼요?) or express your wish (-하고 싶어요). Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Is a refund doable?' 되다 frames it as a feasibility question about store policy — polite and non-confrontational. Real meaning: 'I'd like to return this product and get my money back; is that allowed?'

Said at the counter or service desk of a beauty shop, always in 존댓말. Bring the 영수증 (receipt). The culturally expected order: state the reason first (피부에 안 맞아서, 트러블이 나서), then ask. Going straight to 환불해 주세요 without context can feel abrupt; the 돼요?/가능해요? question softens it.

환불 (money back) vs. 교환 (swap for another item) vs. 반품 (the physical act of returning goods). These are three distinct outcomes. Ask clearly: 환불돼요? for cash back; 교환돼요? to swap. Many shops offer 교환 for opened products even when 환불 is declined.
환불 is Sino-Korean 還拂: 환 (還) = 'to return/give back', 불 (拂) = 'to pay'. Together: 'return payment' = refund.

돈 돌려주세요 ('give back my money') is blunt and confrontational. The civil approach is 환불돼요? / 환불 가능해요?, then 환불하고 싶어요 + reason. Also: 환불하다 is what the store DOES to you; you don't say 제가 환불하고 싶어요 meaning 'I want to refund' — you want to receive a refund.

mistakes: Saying 돈 돌려주세요 to ask for a refund.
That's blunt ('give my money back'). The civil request is 환불돼요? / 환불 가능해요?, then 환불하고 싶어요 with a reason.
Confusing 환불 with 교환.
환불 = money back; 교환 = swap for another item. Ask 환불돼요? for a refund, 교환돼요? to exchange. They're different requests.
Assuming opened cosmetics are returnable.
개봉 (opening) often voids a return. Ask explicitly: 개봉했는데도 환불돼요?, and give a valid reason like 피부에 안 맞아서.

hangul: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요?
english: Can I use this with what I got from the dermatologist?
usage: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요?
Can I use it with my derm products?
Polite; checking compatibility with dermatology items
Is it okay to use together?
Can I apply it with retinol?
레티놀 ('retinol') = a common 'don't mix carelessly' ingredient
examples: A: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? / B: 어떤 성분인지 알면 더 잘 알려드릴 수 있어요.
A: Can I use this with what I got from the dermatologist? / B: If you know the ingredients, I can give you better advice.
Staff may ask about the prescription ingredient — be ready to name it if you know
피부과에서 처방받은 연고 쓰는데 이거 같이 발라도 돼요?
I use a prescribed ointment from the derm — can I apply this with it?
처방받다 ('to be prescribed') + 연고 ('ointment') are the exact words for prescription items
레티놀 쓰는 중인데 이 비타민C랑 같이 쓰면 자극되지 않을까요?
I'm on retinol — won't using it with this vitamin C be irritating?
Naming the active ingredients shows ingredient-layer awareness and gets a precise answer
nuance: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? is 피부과 ('dermatology clinic', Sino-Korean 皮膚科) + 에서 ('from/at') + 받은 거 ('the thing I got') + 랑 ('with') + 같이 ('together') + 써도 돼요? ('is it okay to use?'). This is a real-life advanced layering question. Key vocabulary: 피부과 (the clinic — note 과 '-department/field', as in 내과 'internal medicine', 안과 'ophthalmology'), 처방받다 ('to be prescribed'), 연고 ('ointment'), and the active ingredients people worry about — 레티놀 (retinol), 비타민C (vitamin C), AHA/BHA. The standard skincare layering 순서 in Korea is toner → essence/serum → targeted treatments → cream → sunscreen (morning). The particle structure: the thing you're mixing WITH takes 랑/이랑 (casual) or 와/과 (formal), so 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 means 'together with what I got from the clinic.' The English-speaker errors: (1) omitting 랑/이랑 after 받은 거 — 같이 alone doesn't mark 'with X'; (2) calling the clinic 피부과 의사 when you mean the place — 피부과 = clinic, 피부과 의사/선생님 = the doctor; (3) 함께 사용해도 됩니까? is too formal for a shop. Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Is it okay to use together with what I got from the dermatology clinic?' The real-world question is about ingredient compatibility: will these two products react badly, cancel each other out, or cause irritation when layered together?

Said at a beauty shop when you're on a dermatologist-prescribed routine and want to add an OTC product. 존댓말 with staff. If asking a staff member who isn't a pharmacist or derm, be aware they may not know ingredients deeply — you may also want to check with the prescribing doctor.

같이 써도 괜찮아요? ('is it okay to use together?') is a shorter, vaguer version. 레티놀이랑 같이 발라도 돼요? names the specific ingredient — more precise and more likely to get a useful answer. 순서가 어떻게 돼요? ('what's the layering order?') follows up once compatibility is confirmed.
Simpler: 같이 써도 돼요? Specific ingredient: 레티놀이랑 같이 써도 돼요? Layering order follow-up: 이거 먼저 발라야 돼요 아니면 나중에요? ('should I apply this first or after?')
Omitting 랑/이랑: 같이 alone is 'together' (an adverb), not 'with X' — you need 받은 거랑 같이 to mark what you're mixing with. Also 피부과 = the clinic (place), not the doctor — 피부과 의사/선생님 is the person.

mistakes: Dropping 랑/이랑 and saying 피부과 거 같이 써도 돼요?
'With X' needs the particle 랑/이랑 (casual) or 와/과 (formal): 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? 같이 alone isn't enough to mark 'with what'.
Calling the clinic 피부과 의사 when you mean the place.
피부과 = the dermatology clinic/department; 피부과 의사/선생님 = the doctor (person). To say 'got it at the clinic', 피부과에서 받은 거 is right.
Using 함께 사용해도 됩니까? in a casual shop.
That's stiff and formal. In an everyday beauty shop say 같이 써도 돼요? It carries the same meaning, naturally.

hangul: 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요
english: Help me find a cushion that matches my skin tone
usage: 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요
Find me a cushion for my skin tone
Polite; asking staff to shade-match a cushion/foundation
examples: A: 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요. / B: 피부톤 보니까 21호 쿨톤이 맞을 것 같아요.
A: Help me find a cushion for my skin tone. / B: Looking at your skin, I think a 21 cool-tone would suit you.
The ideal staff shade-match interaction — they assess and recommend
저 21호 쓰는데 좀 밝은 것 같아요. 21.5호 있어요?
I use 21, but it seems a bit light — is there a 21.5?
Half-shades like 21.5호 exist between the main numbers in many Korean lines
저 웜톤이라 핑크 베이스는 떠요. 옐로 베이스로 보여 주세요.
I'm warm-toned, so pink-base looks ashy on me — show me a yellow-base one.
뜨다 ('to float/look ashy') is the precise idiom for a wrong-undertone shade sitting off on the skin
nuance: 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요 is 제 ('my', humble) + 피부톤 ('skin tone') + 에 맞는 ('that matches/suits') + 쿠션 ('cushion compact foundation') + 찾아 주세요 ('please find for me'). Korean base makeup runs on a shade-number system: 13호 (very fair), 21호 (light/fair), 21.5호 (half-step), 23호 (medium), 25호 (deeper) — staff will ask 몇 호 쓰세요? ('what number do you use?'). Undertone vocabulary is 쿨톤 (cool-toned) vs. 웜톤 (warm-toned), part of the huge 퍼스널 컬러 trend; base types are 핑크 베이스 vs. 옐로 베이스. The crucial idiom: 뜨다 ('to float') means a foundation looks ashy, too light, or wrong-undertone on skin (피부에서 떠요 = 'it floats off the skin / looks masky'). 커버력 ('coverage') is the key quality word. The English-speaker error is saying 'shade' as 그림자 ('shadow') — a literal-translation disaster; the right words are 호 (the number) or 색상/톤. Don't say 매치하다 for 'match'; use 에 맞다 ('to suit/fit'). Note 쿠션 here means the cushion-compact makeup format, not a sofa cushion. Default 존댓말; 찾아 주세요 hands the task to staff.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Please find for me a cushion that matches my skin tone.' 맞다 here means 'to fit/suit' — not just visual match but also undertone and finish compatibility. Real meaning: 'I need you to shade-match a cushion foundation to my skin.'

Said at a brand counter or inside Olive Young/Sephora Korea when you need help picking a shade. 존댓말 always with staff. If you already know your number, start with 저 21호예요 — saves time. If you don't know, say 제 피부톤에 맞는 거 추천해 주세요 and let staff assess.

제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요 (open shade-match request) vs. 저 21호예요? 23호예요? (narrowing between specific options) vs. 이거 제 피부톤이랑 맞아요? (checking one product). 뜨다 ('floats/looks ashy') is the key complaint word when a shade is wrong.
More specific: 웜톤에 맞는 쿠션 있어요? Requesting a quality: 커버력 좋은 걸로 찾아 주세요. Asking about finish: 매트한 거로 추천해 주세요 ('recommend a matte one') vs. 광 나는 거 ('a dewy/glow one').

Saying 그림자 ('shadow') for a makeup 'shade' is a complete translation error — it means a literal shadow. A foundation shade is 호 (number) or 색상/톤. Also: 뜨다 ('floats') is the specific idiom for a wrong shade — not 안 어울려요 ('doesn't suit'), which is too general.

mistakes: Saying 그림자 ('shadow') for a makeup 'shade'.
그림자 is a literal shadow. A foundation shade is a number 호 (21호, 23호) or 색상/톤. Ask 몇 호가 맞아요? not anything with 그림자.
Using Sino vs. native numbers wrongly with 호.
Shade numbers use Sino-Korean: 21호 = 이십일 호, 23호 = 이십삼 호. Say 이십일 호, not native 스물한. The counter 호 takes Sino numbers.
Translating 'it doesn't match / looks off' as 안 어울려요 only.
안 어울려요 ('doesn't suit') is general. For a foundation that sits wrong/looks ashy, the precise idiom is 떠요 ('it floats'): 피부에서 떠요.

usage: 각질 정리 ('tidying dead skin') for a gentle ask
examples: A: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요. / B: 주 1~2회 각질 제거제 쓰시고 충분히 보습하시면 나아질 거예요.
A: My skin keeps flaking. / B: Use an exfoliant once or twice a week and moisturize well — that should help.
The natural complaint-and-advice exchange on dry skin flaking
화장하면 각질이 다 일어나서 들떠요. 어떻게 해야 돼요?
When I do makeup, the flakes lift and it cakes — what should I do?
들뜨다 ('to lift/cake') is the specific makeup-over-flakes complaint
각질 제거하고 싶은데 너무 자극적이지 않은 거 있어요? 저 민감성이라서요.
I want to exfoliate but nothing too harsh — I have sensitive skin.
Asking for gentle exfoliation given sensitivity; 자극적 ('harsh/irritating') is the key qualifier
nuance: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요 is 각질 ('dead skin cells / flaky skin', Sino-Korean 角質) + 이 + 자꾸 ('repeatedly, keeps happening') + 일어나요 (from 일어나다, here meaning 'to lift up / flake'). 각질 is THE word for dead-skin flakiness; it pairs with fixed verbs: 각질이 일어나다 ('skin flakes/peels up'), 각질 제거 ('exfoliation'), 각질 정리 (a gentler 'tidying/smoothing'). Exfoliating products include 필링 (peeling pad/gel), 스크럽 (scrub), 각질 제거제 (exfoliant). The related makeup problem is 들뜨다 ('to lift/cake') — when foundation sits on top of flakes and looks patchy; don't confuse this with 뜨다 ('to look ashy', a shade problem). For severe dryness: 갈라지다 ('to crack/split') and 트다 ('to chap', especially 입술이 트다 'chapped lips'). 자꾸 conveys the frustrating, recurring nature — it's what makes this phrase feel real rather than clinical. The English-speaker error is using 벗겨지다 ('to be peeled off', like sunburned skin) for ongoing dry flaking — 벗겨지다 fits a sunburn or a peel mask result; everyday dry flaking is 각질이 일어나다. Another trap: 죽은 피부 ('dead skin') sounds morbid and medical — the cosmetic word is 각질. Particle: 각질이 일어나다 (subject marker 이/가). Default 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Dead-skin-cells keep rising up.' 각질 (角質) = 'horny/keratinous substance' (the clinical Sino-Korean term). 일어나다 usually means 'to get up/rise' but also 'to lift up', giving the vivid image of flakes lifting off the skin surface. Real meaning: 'My skin keeps peeling and flaking — I can't get rid of it.'

Said to a beauty clerk or in a skincare consultation when describing a persistent dryness problem. 존댓말 with staff. The word 자꾸 ('keeps doing it') signals the problem is recurring, not just today — important context for getting the right product recommendation.

각질이 일어나다 (dry flaking, ongoing) vs. 벗겨지다 (peeling off in sheets, like sunburn) vs. 갈라지다 (cracking, severe dryness). 들뜨다 (foundation cakes over flakes) is the makeup-specific consequence. 트다 (chapping) is for lips and hands specifically.
각질 is Sino-Korean 角質 ('horny/keratinous substance') — the cosmetic term for dead-skin flakiness. 각질 제거 adds 제거 (除去) = 'removal': exfoliation.

벗겨지다 ('to be peeled off') fits sunburn sloughing or a peel mask; it's too dramatic for everyday dry flaking. Use 각질이 일어나다. Also: 죽은 피부 ('dead skin' literal translation) sounds morbid; the cosmetic term is 각질 only.

mistakes: Saying 죽은 피부 for 'dead skin'.
죽은 피부 ('dead skin') sounds morbid/medical. The cosmetic term for flaky dead-skin cells is 각질: 각질이 일어나요, 각질 제거.
Using 벗겨지다 for everyday dry flaking.
벗겨지다 ('to be peeled off') fits sunburn sloughing or a peel-mask result. Ongoing dry flaking is 각질이 일어나다. Say 각질이 일어나요.
Confusing 들뜨다 (makeup cakes) with 뜨다 (wrong shade).
들뜨다 = foundation lifts/cakes over flakes; 뜨다 = a shade looks ashy/floats. For flaking-related caking, use 들떠요.
